summary: Describes version 1.0 of the Referral Whois (RWhois) client/server protocol, a distributed system for looking up hierarchical information such as domain and network contacts. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2167.

eli5.summary: Instead of one giant address book, you get pointed from book to book until you find the right entry.

subtitle: A distributed system for looking up network and domain registration information

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, a centralized WHOIS database became a bottleneck. A single registry could not handle the volume of lookups for network numbers, domains, and administrative contacts, and distributed registries had no standard way to refer queries to the right authority.
tldr.mechanism: RWhois (Referral WHOIS) implements a hierarchical, distributed system where servers can refer clients to other servers that have authority over more specific information, reducing load on central registries and allowing regional registries to maintain their own data.
tldr.outcome: RWhois provided a protocol for distributed lookups but was later replaced by more comprehensive solutions. RFC 2167 superseded it with improvements to the protocol specification.

today: RFC 1714 is historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 2167, which provides an improved version of the RWhois specification. However, the hierarchical referral approach pioneered by RWhois remains relevant in modern distributed directory systems.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 1714 describes version 1.0 of the RWhois (Referral WHOIS) protocol, an improvement over the original WHOIS system defined in RFC 954. The original WHOIS service, maintained by the SRI-NIC, was a centralized database for host names, network information, and user contact details. As the Internet grew to hundreds of thousands of systems, this centralized approach became inefficient.

RWhois solves this problem by implementing a hierarchical system that mirrors the structure of the Internet itself. Instead of querying a single central server, a client can query any server in the hierarchy, and that server will either answer the query or refer the client to a more authoritative server. This reduces load on the central registry and allows regional registries (like RIPE NCC for Europe and APNIC for Asia-Pacific) to maintain and serve their own data independently.
sections.eli5: The Internet got too big for one address book. RWhois lets different regions keep their own lists and refer you to each other.

sections.title: Hierarchical and Distributed Design
sections.content:
The information that registries maintain is inherently hierarchical. For example, hammer.nic.ddn.mil is part of nic.ddn.mil, which is part of ddn.mil, which is part of .mil. Similarly, IP address 198.41.0.21 is part of network 198.41.0.0/24, which is part of 198.41.0.0/16, and so on.

RWhois takes advantage of this hierarchy. When a client queries a server that does not have the authority for a particular domain or IP block, the server can reduce the query and refer the client to a more specific authority. The protocol supports three types of referrals: link referrals (same authority, different server), reduction referrals (more specific authority), and punt referrals (server cannot answer and refers to a higher level).
sections.eli5: Information is organized like a tree. A server can say 'I don't know about this specific leaf, but try the server over here that handles that branch.'

sections.title: Client and Server Interaction
sections.content:
RWhois defines directives that clients send to servers and responses that servers send back. Clients send directives prefixed with a hyphen (e.g., -RWhois V-1.0) to identify themselves as RWhois clients and request specific services. Required directives include the query itself and the -RWhois identifier.

Servers respond with prefixed responses (e.g., %referral, %ok, %error). The %referral response tells the client to query another server, potentially one that is a standard RFC 954 WHOIS or WHOIS++ server. RWhois is designed to be backward compatible with the original WHOIS protocol, so an RWhois server can respond to queries from old WHOIS clients, and RWhois clients can interact with old WHOIS servers.
sections.eli5: Clients say 'I'm looking for information about X' and servers say either 'Here it is' or 'Try asking that server instead.'

sections.title: Key Features and Extensions
sections.content:
RWhois supports optional directives for advanced functions. The -schema directive lets clients discover what types of data a server holds and what attributes each object type has. The -xfer directive allows bulk data transfer for caching at secondary servers. The -load directive lets clients check server load before committing to a query.

The protocol includes registration capabilities through the -register directive, allowing authorized clients to add, modify, or delete objects in the database. The -notify directive lets clients report bad referrals or recursive loops to servers, improving the accuracy and reliability of the distributed system. The protocol also supports extensions through the -X- prefix, allowing private or new public directives to be added without modifying the core specification.
sections.eli5: Beyond just looking things up, RWhois lets you discover what a server knows, update information, report problems, and add new kinds of lookups.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes compatibility with the original WHOIS protocol. An RWhois server must respond to basic WHOIS queries from standard clients. The RWhois client must wait for an %RWhois response to confirm it is talking to an RWhois server before sending extended directives; if the response does not come, the client falls back to standard WHOIS behavior.

RWhois servers maintain authority for specific areas (domains, IP address blocks). Secondary servers can cache data from primary servers and are kept in sync through notifications and periodic data transfers. The specification includes error codes to handle various failure conditions, from invalid directives to exceeding query limits.
sections.eli5: RWhois servers have to work like old WHOIS servers too. They keep track of who they're responsible for, and secondary servers can get copies of the data.
